idiom_name: orm.composite() binding one attribute to several mapped columns
implementation_notes: SQLAlchemy names the pattern composite(): a set of columns is associated with a single user-defined datatype (in modern use a dataclass), and the ORM exposes one attribute that represents the group. The mapping is declarative - composite(mapped_column("x1"), mapped_column("y1")) - and the columns are also usable individually in queries and WHERE criteria, which is the pattern's promise of column-level predicates. The one documented trap is change detection: by default the composite object must be replaced for an UPDATE to be emitted, and in-place mutation needs the Mutation Tracking extension. Dataclass composites are fully supported since 2.0, including deriving column types from the class.
pitfalls: In-place mutation of the composite is not detected: assigning a new Point emits the UPDATE, mutating point.x does not - use the Mutation Tracking extension if callers expect setters to work.

A composite can be used as a SQL expression in WHERE criteria, but the comparison is implemented by SQLAlchemy's Comparator, not by the dataclass's __eq__, so do not rely on custom comparison methods in queries.
The composite attribute and the underlying columns are both visible on the class: writing to the columns directly bypasses the value object and can leave it stale.

variants.name: Django flat columns with a custom Field or descriptor
variants.idiom_name: flat model fields plus a custom Field/descriptor that converts to the value object
variants.implementation_notes: Django ships no embedded-value mapping: a Django model attribute is one column, so the documented route for a complex Python object is a Field subclass whose from_db_value/get_prep_value convert between the value object and the stored representation, or - for a value spread over several columns, which is what Embedded Value means - separate flat fields plus a property/descriptor that composes them into the value object. The database layout is therefore the pattern's, but the decompose/recompose pair is application code; use this when the value is genuinely multi-column and Django is already the stack, and prefer a single custom Field when the value fits one column (which is Serialized LOB, not Embedded Value).
pitfalls: A property is not a queryable field: filtering by the value object itself is not possible, so callers must know the underlying column names - the decomposition leaks exactly where Django has no composite support.
Saving a model with only the property assigned does not mark the flat fields dirty unless they are set on the instance, so bulk update() and partial saves can write stale columns.
Subclassing Field for a multi-column value does not work - a Field maps to one column; use a descriptor or several fields instead, otherwise you have built a Serialized LOB by accident.
